analysis.one_liner: Bans pharmacy benefit managers from paying kickbacks to win employer drug plan contracts.
analysis.headline: The House Education and Workforce Committee approved the bill unanimously, 34 to 0, and placed it on the House calendar on July 2, 2026, but the full House has not voted and the bill has no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) are middlemen that run prescription drug plans for employers and insurers. This bill adds a rule to the federal law governing employee benefit plans barring a PBM from paying anyone for the referral, placement, retention, or renewal of plan business, or for shaping how plans are bid out. It also presumes that payments PBMs make to brokers and consultants are kickbacks unless the parties can document in writing that the pay reflects fair market value for real services. The goal is to strip hidden side payments out of drug plan contracting so that what plans and workers pay for medicine reflects actual drug prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees in employer health plans, and the employers who sponsor those plans, gain the most: the bill targets the side payments that can inflate the cost of drug coverage and are effectively financed through premiums and drug prices. Brokers and consultants who compete on genuine services rather than contingent payments also gain a cleaner market.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends ERISA section 408 to prohibit any direct or indirect compensation paid by a PBM to an individual or entity for the referral, recommendation, placement, retention, or renewal of plan business, or for inclusion or participation in the design of a request for proposal, market check, evaluation, or any other contracting process. [S2]
It prevents PBMs from relabeling kickbacks to evade the ban: compensation is judged by its economic substance and practical operation, not by what the contract calls it. [S2]

It shifts the burden of proof: payments from a PBM to a broker, consultant, advisor, or related entity are presumed to be for referral or contracting influence unless contemporaneous written documentation shows the pay is fair market value for bona fide services. [S2]
The rule applies to plan years beginning after enactment, so new contracts would have to comply going forward. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: PBM companies lose the ability to pay for contract wins and face new legal exposure on existing payment structures. Benefits brokers and consultants who rely on contingent or volume-based fees lose that compensation stream, and employers bear modest new documentation costs.

drawbacks.text: The presumption of a kickback for any broker or consultant payment could chill legitimate consulting arrangements, since the parties must produce contemporaneous written documentation proving fair market value for bona fide services or the payment is treated as a prohibited kickback. [S2]

The bill reaches only one channel of PBM economics: payments a PBM makes to win or keep plan business. It does not cap what PBMs charge plans, disclose their negotiated prices, or restructure the rebate flows between drug manufacturers and PBMs, so it may not lower drug costs on its own. [S2]

Enforcement depends on plan sponsors and the Labor Department pursuing violations under the ERISA prohibited-transaction framework; the bill creates the rule but no new enforcement funding or private remedy beyond what ERISA already provides. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core rule is a targeted anti-kickback provision for the drug plan middleman market, and the people it protects — workers and employers paying for drug coverage — far outnumber the firms that lose the fee streams. The main honest costs are compliance and documentation burdens on the broker industry and the risk that the presumption against broker payments sweeps in ordinary services. Its practical impact on what families actually pay at the pharmacy depends on how the largest PBMs restructure their contracts, which the bill does not directly command.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it unanimously and put it on the House's calendar in July 2026, but no full House vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Rick Allen (R-GA) introduced the bill on March 12, 2026, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce. [S1] [S4]
The committee held a markup on May 21, 2026, and ordered the bill reported as amended by a bipartisan vote of 34 to 0. [S4]
The committee reported the amended bill on July 2, 2026 (H. Rept. 119-729), and it was placed on the Union Calendar, which is where bills wait to be scheduled for a floor vote. [S4]
As of the latest action record, no further House action has been taken — the bill sits on the calendar awaiting a scheduling decision by House leadership. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No outcome yet. If the bill stays on the calendar without a floor vote, the parties better off are the PBM firms and benefits brokers whose fee arrangements would otherwise be restricted, since the current rules remain in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Undecided; PBM firms if it stalls

for.name: Rep. Rick W. Allen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through committee, where it was amended and reported 34-0.

for.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
for.what_they_did: Held a markup, amended the bill, and ordered it reported 34 to 0, then reported it with H. Rept. 119-729.

sides.party_line_note: The committee approved the bill 34 to 0 with no recorded opposition, and no member has spoken against it in the record; the absence of any floor vote is the remaining obstacle.

industries.note: The bill bars PBMs from paying for referrals, contract placement, and influence over bidding processes, and judges payments by substance rather than label, striking at fee structures built into how the largest PBMs win and keep plan business. The cost of those payments ultimately flows into what plans and workers pay for drugs, so the industry's interest runs against the public's here.

Payments PBMs make to brokers and consultants are presumed kickbacks unless documented in writing at fair market value for bona fide services, making contingent and volume-based fee arrangements difficult to maintain. Ordinary consumers may benefit from cleaner advice as a result.
Plan sponsors gain a contracting process stripped of side payments, which should make PBM pricing more reflective of actual drug costs. That saving is shared with the workers covered by the plans.

analysis.trajectory: The bill cleared committee unanimously but has no cosponsors and has sat on the Union Calendar since July 2026 with no floor vote scheduled. Most House bills on the calendar never reach the floor unless leadership schedules them, and as a standalone measure late in the session its most realistic paths are attachment to a broader package or stalling until the Congress ends.
